items.title: Porter's framework asks about industry structure, not firms
items.claim: Michael Porter's 1979 HBR article introduced the five forces framework. What does it analyse?

options.text: The structural attractiveness of an industry: rivalry, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes

items.reveal:
Porter's 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy' (HBR, March 1979) made a structural argument: average industry profitability is set by the strength of the five forces. Some industries (pharma, software platforms) are persistently profitable; others (airlines, supermarkets) persistently low-margin.

McGahan and Porter (1997) found industry effects explained 19% of business unit profitability variance — less than firm effects (32%) but real. Critics (including Henry Mintzberg) argue the framework underweights innovation, complementors and network effects, which 1979 industry economics didn't see clearly.
items.why: Strategy starts with which industry you're competing in, not how cleverly you compete. Some industries make it nearly impossible to earn supernormal returns.

items.title: First-mover advantage is more often a myth than a rule
items.claim: Gerard Tellis and Peter Golder studied first movers across 50 product categories. What did they find?

options.text: First movers won permanently in nearly all categories
About 47% of first movers failed and the average market share of survivors was around 10%; long-term winners were more often early followers than pioneers

items.reveal:
Tellis and Golder's 'Will and Vision' (2002) and earlier paper analysed product categories from photocopiers to disposable nappies. Pioneers identified: Chux nappies (replaced by Pampers); WordStar (overtaken by Word); Friendster and MySpace (overtaken by Facebook); AltaVista (overtaken by Google).

Later entrants benefit from market education done by pioneers, technology improvements, and clearer customer preferences. The 'first mover advantage' framing oversells a narrow set of cases (network-effect platforms) as if it were general.
items.why: Business teaching often treats first-mover advantage as a strategic prize. Empirical work suggests being the right mover at the right time is more important than being first.

items.title: The 7Ps were extended for services, not because the 4Ps were wrong
items.claim: The original 4Ps (product, price, place, promotion) were proposed by E. Jerome McCarthy in 1960. Why were three more Ps added later?

options.text: Booms and Bitner (1981) added people, process and physical evidence to capture the special characteristics of service industries (intangibility, inseparability, variability, perishability)
Because digital marketing required four extra Ps

items.reveal:
Bernard Booms and Mary Bitner's 1981 chapter 'Marketing Strategies and Organization Structures for Service Firms' added People (staff interactions with customers), Process (service delivery procedures) and Physical evidence (the tangible elements customers see).

A haircut, a flight or a consultation can't be inventoried, tested or returned. The 4Ps work better for tangible goods than for services, which by 2020 made up around 80% of UK GDP.
items.why: Frameworks evolve as the economy does. The 7Ps reflect a shift toward services that has continued since 1981.
